Article Title: 2 strategic satellites sit at spaceport as govt nod eludes Isro
Article Text:
GSLV-Mk2

BENGALURU: Two strategically important satellites, NVS-03 and Gisat-1A, have been sitting at India’s spaceport in Sriharikota for weeks, awaiting govt approval for launch. Also waiting is a GSLV-Mk2 rocket, whose propellant filling was halted midway after launch clearance failed to come through, multiple sources told TOI.The delay comes even as the govt is yet to publicly disclose detailed findings into the failures of two PSLV missions — May 18, 2025 and Jan 12, 2026 — that have effectively slowed India’s launch programme across vehicle families.Sources said NVS-03, the next satellite in India's second-generation NavIC navigation constellation, and GISAT-1A or EOS-05, an advanced geo-imaging satellite capable of near real-time observation of the Indian landmass, have both completed most pre-launch preparations and are ready for flight.The GSLV-Mk2 at the spaceport was designated for one of the missions (NVS-03 or Gisat-1A). The pause in launch follows a difficult year for Isro. On Jan 12, PSLV-C62 failed to place its payloads into orbit after a disruption in the third stage (PS3).Eight months before that, PSLV-C61 had also failed because of what Isro has described only as a “pressure drop in PS3”. Apart from these brief descriptions, neither the department of space (DoS) nor the Govt has released detailed failure reports.Union minister Jitendra Singh recently said in Bengaluru that the failure analysis committee investigating the PSLV-C62 mission had identified the cause of the anomaly but that the findings “could not be disclosed publicly”.The apparent caution extending beyond PSLV has befuddled even those within the Department of Space, which is already battling low morale. Officials familiar with the matter said no launches have been cleared while the govt reviews the situation.Pointing out that the issues identified so far relate specifically to the PSLV’s third stage and do not directly involve either the GSLV or the LVM-3, one insider said: “We don’t get the logic. It’s like telling us not to take our cars out because our bike had an issue in its previous outing.” The person argued that GSLV and LVM rockets don’t borrow anything from the PSLV third stage.The delay is particularly significant because both satellites have strategic roles. NVS-03 is expected to be one step in reviving the now-defunct NavIC navigation constellation. Even the govt last week admitted that with just three functional satellites, the NavIC programme has failed to deliver navigation services for lack of satellites.Gisat-1A, meanwhile, revives a mission that has suffered repeated setbacks. The original Gisat-1, India’s first geostationary Earth observation satellite designed to provide frequent imaging of the subcontinent, was first delayed in 2020 before being lost during the GSLV-F10 mission in Aug 2021 after the cryogenic upper stage failed to ignite. The replacement spacecraft is expected to provide near real-time imaging for disaster management, agriculture, forestry, environmental monitoring and national security.The govt’s caution follows another major setback that was investigated in detail. Isro, in Feb this year, released partial findings into the Jan 2025 NVS-02 anomaly, concluding that the spacecraft failed to reach its intended orbit because the drive signal never reached the pyro valve in the oxidiser line during orbit-raising manoeuvres.The agency said corrective measures had since been implemented and successfully validated on the CMS-03 mission launched aboard LVM-3 in Nov 2025. For now, however, even as hardware, satellites and launch vehicles stand ready at the spaceport, India’s next launches remain on hold, with no indication of when the govt will authorise launches to resume.
Article Summary: Two strategically important satellites, nvs-03 and gisat-1a, have been sitting at india’s spaceport in sriharikota for weeks. Also waiting is a gslv-mk2 rocket, whose propellant filling was halted midway after launch clearance failed to come through. Delay comes even as the govt is yet to publicly disclose detailed findings into the failures of two pslv missions.

Article Title: Educated but unemployed: Inside India's broken jobs market and why the 'cockroaches' are fed up
Article Text:
India's un-employment crisis and helplessness of modern life. (Representative image)

And at its heart lies a simple question. What happens when an economy produces millions of graduates every year but fails to create enough quality jobs?

India's employment challenge



The problem isn't just unemployment, it's job quality



Why educated youth feel left behind

India's employment paradox



Is India creating enough jobs?



The informal sector is slowing too



India's employment quality lags behind peers



The real issue is the lack of decent employment opportunities. We saw this clearly in Uttar Pradesh in 2017, when more than two lakh people applied for peon posts. Many applicants held qualifications such as PhDs, MTech, BTech, MCom and BCom degrees. When highly educated people apply for peon jobs, it shows they are unable to find work that matches their qualifications. Arun Kumar

AI adds a new challenge



India's demographic dividend at a crossroads



When NEET became the tipping point

Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis transformed an ordinary man into a giant insect to explore alienation, helplessness and the dehumanising pressures of modern life.More than a century later, India's self-styled Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has adopted a similarly unsettling symbol, not to tell a work of fiction, but to express the frustrations of a generation increasingly unsure whether years of education, expensive coaching and relentless competition will ever translate into a stable job.What began as a social media sensation with a strong and straightforward satirical structure, quickly evolved into one of the country's biggest youth-led movements in recent years.Calling itself the "voice of the lazy and unemployed," the movement grew from memes mocking joblessness, paper leaks, inflation and the political establishment into street protests.The protest may have become a trigger for a generation already grappling with shrinking employment opportunities, rising educational costs and growing uncertainty about the future.According to veteran economist Arun Kumar , a retired professor at JNU, "This unemployment crisis has created a huge gap between expectations and reality.""Young people earn degrees believing they will secure good jobs, but when those jobs do not materialise, they continue preparing for competitive examinations year after year. Many take these exams four, five or even six times because they still hope to secure an organised sector job.Their parents also encourage them because they know such jobs offer stable salaries and social security," he said."But the increasing privatisation of education has intensified competition. Coaching institutes want to showcase high success rates because that is their biggest selling point. That creates incentives for unethical practices, including paper leaks. The greater the privatisation, the greater the pressure to resort to illegal methods to ensure students succeed. Fake degrees, cheating and question paper leaks are all symptoms of a much deeper problem. They are linked to unemployment and the shortage of quality jobs in the organised sector," he added.India has spent decades expanding access to higher education. Universities have multiplied, enrollment has surged and millions of families have invested heavily in degrees, viewing education as the surest path to upward mobility.The numbers tell a remarkable story. According to the State of Working India 2026 report by Azim Premji University, the number of young graduates in India increased nearly 13-fold, rising from around 5 million in 1983 to 63 million in 2023.But while the supply of graduates has grown rapidly, employment opportunities have not kept pace.The report estimates that graduate unemployment among people below the age of 25 is now close to 40%, while graduates accounted for nearly two-thirds of India's unemployed population in 2023.Even more striking is the rise in the number of unemployed graduates, which has increased from less than one million in 1983 to around 11 million in 2023, a 16-fold increase over four decades.The mismatch between education and employment has widened steadily since the mid-2000s as higher education expanded much faster than the creation of quality jobs. For millions of families, earning a college degree no longer guarantees stable employment or financial security.Recent government data suggest that the challenge is becoming even more severe.According to the government's flagship Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 rose to 16.2% in June, the highest level recorded since monthly estimates became available in April 2025. At that time, youth unemployment stood at 13.8%.The ministry of statistics and programme implementation (MoSPI) has cautioned that monthly figures may fluctuate because of seasonal factors, academic cycles and the increased frequency of surveys.Even so, the latest numbers are significant because they fit into a broader pattern rather than representing an isolated spike. Youth unemployment has increased across all six categories tracked by the survey, urban and rural areas, men and women alike, during the 15 months for which monthly data are available.At the same time, the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) among young people has declined from 42.7% to 40.3%. In simple terms, fewer young people are actively looking for work.Ordinarily, such a decline would be expected to reduce unemployment because fewer people are participating in the labour market. Instead, unemployment has continued to rise, suggesting that the economy is not generating enough opportunities even for the shrinking pool of job seekers.Annual PLFS data reinforce the same trend. Between 2022 and 2025, youth unemployment increased in 13 states and Union Territories, including Andhra Pradesh, Delhi, Telangana and West Bengal.The situation appears even more challenging for young women, with unemployment rising across 16 states and Union Territories during the same period.Taken together, the figures suggest that youth unemployment is becoming a structural challenge rather than a temporary fluctuation.Headline unemployment figures often fail to capture the deeper challenges within India's labour market. Many graduates do find work, but not necessarily the kind of work they expected after spending years in higher education.Economist Arun Kumar said that the root of the problem is the sharp divide between India's organised and unorganised sectors."When unemployment rises, it inevitably leads to greater conflict because there are too few jobs for too many people. In India, this problem is even more pronounced because the unorganised sector employs around 94% of the workforce, while the organised sector employs only about 6%. The difference in wages and job security between these two sectors is enormous. A courier delivery worker may earn around Rs 10,000-12,000 a month, whereas a postman can earn around Rs 70,000. Naturally, nobody wants to lose an organised sector job, and everyone wants to secure one. That intense competition creates immense pressure," he added.An analysis of India's Periodic Labour Force Survey illustrates this disconnect. Out of every 100 graduates aged between 15 and 29, only 50 are employed, 15 remain unemployed while actively searching for work, and the remaining 35 are outside the labour force altogether.Some continue their education. Others perform unpaid domestic work or have simply stopped looking for employment after repeated disappointments.Even among those who are employed, the quality of jobs remains a major concern. Only 26 out of every 100 graduates have regular salaried jobs. More strikingly, just four hold formal jobs that provide written contracts, paid leave and social security benefits.The remaining graduates are spread across self-employment, unpaid family work, casual labour and small household enterprises. Many earn irregular incomes and lack job security despite years spent pursuing higher education.The figures highlight a growing reality in India's labour market: employment alone is no longer an adequate measure of economic well-being. The challenge is increasingly about the availability of secure, productive and reasonably paid jobs.The employment crisis begins long before students enter the labour market. Competition for limited seats in prestigious colleges has transformed education itself into an expensive investment.Government survey data show that Indian households now spend a significantly larger share of their education budgets on private coaching than they did seven years ago.The sharpest increase has been among higher secondary students preparing for engineering, medical and university entrance examinations.Families now spend nearly one-fourth of their higher secondary education budgets on coaching, compared with about 18% in 2018.Private coaching expenses have also increased steadily across primary, middle and secondary education, reflecting a growing belief that classroom teaching alone is no longer sufficient to compete in high-stakes entrance examinations.The pressure becomes particularly visible in engineering education. India had around 4.4 million undergraduate engineering students during the 2023-24 academic year. Yet the country's top 100 engineering institutions together offered only about 500,000 seats.In effect, only one in nine engineering students can study at an institution widely regarded as offering strong placements and better career prospects.Students who fail to secure admission to elite institutions often graduate from colleges with weaker placement records, making it significantly harder to obtain well-paying jobs.The widening gap between educational aspirations and employment outcomes has created growing frustration among young people. The traditional promise that more education automatically leads to better employment is becoming increasingly uncertain.According to the State of Working India 2026 report, fewer than 7% of male graduates secure a permanent salaried job within one year of graduating. The figure is even lower, just 3.7%, when it comes to white-collar jobs.Using data from the PLFS and the earlier Employment-Unemployment Survey, the report estimates that 1.1 crore out of India's 6.3 crore graduates aged between 20 and 29 were unemployed in 2023.Graduate unemployment itself is not a new phenomenon. The report estimates that unemployment among graduates below the age of 25 increased from 35.02% in 1983 to 39.33% in 2023.What has changed, however, is the scale of the problem. India now produces far more graduates than ever before, while simultaneously entering the most important phase of its demographic transition.The country's median age currently stands at around 29 years and is expected to rise to 38 years by 2050.This is the period during which India's working-age population is expected to drive economic growth. If the economy fails to generate enough productive employment during this demographic window, the much-discussed demographic dividend could gradually turn into a demographic challenge.India today is one of the world's fastest-growing major economies. Even amid geopolitical tensions, volatile oil prices and slowing global trade, the country has continued to post robust GDP growth and position itself as a manufacturing and investment hub.The government has invested heavily in highways, airports, railways, ports and digital infrastructure. Global technology companies such as Apple have expanded manufacturing in India, electronics exports have surged and semiconductor investments are beginning to gather pace.Policymakers increasingly see manufacturing as the sector that can absorb millions of workers and turn India's demographic advantage into sustained economic growth.Yet for many young Indians entering the labour market, this optimism feels distant. The central contradiction facing the Indian economy is that rapid economic growth has not translated into an equivalent expansion in quality employment.Economists often describe this phenomenon as "jobless growth", an economy that continues to grow without creating enough secure and productive jobs.India's challenge is especially daunting because nearly eight million graduates enter the labour market every year. Generating employment for such a large number of educated young people has become one of the country's biggest economic challenges.This gap between economic growth and employment opportunities lies at the heart of the frustration that has fuelled recent youth protests.Whether India is creating enough jobs depends largely on which dataset is examined. The Reserve Bank of India's KLEMS database estimated that the economy generated 4.7 crore jobs during 2023-24, the highest annual increase in more than four decades.However, labour economists caution against looking at headline employment numbers alone.Employment estimates differ across official surveys because they use different methodologies. More importantly, the definition of employment itself often masks the underlying quality of jobs being created.For instance, India's labour surveys classify a person as employed if they have worked even for a few days during the reference period.Likewise, unpaid family workers and subsistence self-employed individuals are counted as employed despite earning little or no regular income.As a result, headline employment figures may paint a healthier picture than what many young workers experience in reality. Increasingly, economists argue that the more important question is no longer how many jobs India is creating, but what kind of jobs they are.For decades, India's informal economy acted as a safety valve for the labour market. Workers unable to secure formal employment often found opportunities in small businesses, family enterprises, retail trade or self-employment.However, even this safety net appears to be weakening.According to the ministry of statistics and programme implementation's latest Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), the informal sector generated around 74.5 lakh jobs in 2025, significantly lower than the 1.1 crore jobs created during the previous survey period ending September 2024.Wage growth has also slowed sharply. Average wage growth in the sector declined to 3.9%, compared with 13% previously, suggesting that even workers who manage to find employment are seeing slower improvements in earnings.The figures reinforce concerns that employment opportunities are weakening across both formal and informal sectors, making it increasingly difficult for young people to find stable livelihoods.India's labour market also differs from many comparable economies because of the quality of employment available.International comparisons reveal another structural weakness: the quality of employment. Labour market studies show that around 93% of employed workers in Russia hold regular jobs. The share is about 68% in Brazil, 54% in China and 42% in Bangladesh, the PLFS 2022-23 & Jan-Mar 2024 data reported.In India, by contrast, only about 23% of workers are in regular salaried employment.This means that nearly three-fourths of Indian workers remain outside the formal sector, without written contracts, paid leave, provident fund benefits or social security.The shortage of secure employment also explains the extraordinary demand for government jobs. Whether it is railways, banking, the armed forces, civil services or state recruitmentexaminations, millions of candidates compete for relatively few vacancies because government employment still offers something much of the private sector cannot consistently provide stability.A government job often brings predictable salaries, pensions, housing allowances, healthcare benefits and long-term security.For many young Indians, particularly those from middle- and lower-income households, these jobs represent far more than employment. They represent financial stability for entire families.According to Kumar, the desperation is visible in the jobs educated Indians are willing to apply for.Even as India grapples with creating quality jobs, technological change is reshaping the employment landscape.A government-backed research group estimates that artificial intelligence could displace around three million managerial and coding jobs by the end of this decade.Automation is expected to reduce demand for routine white-collar work at a time when India is producing record numbers of engineering and technology graduates.Overseas opportunities are also becoming more limited. Tighter immigration policies in countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia have reduced opportunities for skilled Indian professionals.For decades, migration acted as a safety valve for India's educated workforce. That pathway is becoming increasingly uncertain."Many young Indians even leave the country in search of better opportunities. Some spend lakhs of rupees to migrate, while others take illegal routes because they see very few prospects at home. In many cases, they still end up doing low-paying or menial jobs abroad. That reflects the level of desperation created by the lack of opportunities in India,"Kumar noted on the brain-drain situation in India.India possesses one of the world's youngest populations, a demographic advantage that economists have long viewed as one of the country's greatest strengths.A growing working-age population has the potential to accelerate economic growth, boost productivity and expand domestic consumption.But demographic dividends are never automatic. They depend on whether an economy can generate enough productive employment for the millions entering the labour market every year.Research suggests that India's employment intensity of growth, the ability of economic expansion to generate jobs has steadily declined over the past four decades.Against this backdrop, the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak became much more than an examination controversy. Millions of students spend months and often years preparing for the country's most competitive entrance examinations.Families invest heavily in coaching classes, relocate to education hubs and, in many cases, students take gap years in pursuit of a medical seat.When allegations emerged that the examination paper had been leaked and sold before the test, the issue struck at the heart of a system that already demanded enormous financial and emotional investment.The government cancelled the examination, handed the investigation to the Central Bureau of Investigation and ordered a re-examination.For lakhs of aspirants, particularly those from middle- and lower-income households, the cancellation meant far more than repeating a test. It meant another year of uncertainty after months of preparation and considerable financial sacrifice.Some students performed worse in the re-examination. Others worried they had lost their best chance of securing admission. Reports of severe psychological stress and alleged student suicides linked to the controversy further intensified public anger.What began as protests against examination irregularities gradually evolved into a wider movement about education, unemployment and shrinking opportunities.It was in this atmosphere that the Cockroach Janta Party found resonance among young Indians. Initially known for satirical social media posts, the movement soon expanded into organised protests questioning paper leaks, unemployment, inflation and what participants described as the growing disconnect between educational aspirations and employment opportunities.The group's unusual symbol, the cockroach, captured widespread attention.The insect represented resilience, survival and invisibility, mirroring how many young people felt overlooked despite years of education and preparation. Eventually, the protests became one of the biggest youth movements witnessed in recent years.The protests exposed far more than frustration over one examination. They revealed a widening disconnect between education, employment and economic expectations.Economist Arun Kumar says unemployment extends far beyond those who are officially counted as jobless."Youth unemployment, particularly among those aged 15 to 29, is extremely high, and the situation is especially difficult for women. There are different forms of unemployment. First, there are those actively looking for work but unable to find it. Second, there are people who are technically employed but only in low-paid, part-time or menial jobs that do not provide a decent livelihood," he said."Third, there is disguised unemployment, where people appear to be working but contribute little to productive economic activity. Finally, there are those who have stopped looking for work altogether because they have lost hope. Women are disproportionately represented in this last category. Female labour force participation in India remains much lower than in many other major economies, which means many women are no longer even counted among active job seekers," he added.Over the past few decades, India has dramatically expanded access to higher education, produced record numbers of graduates and remained one of the world's fastest-growing major economies.But the growth in quality jobs has failed to keep pace with the growing pool of educated youth. For many young Indians, securing a degree no longer guarantees a stable career or upward social mobility.That gap between aspirations and opportunities lies at the heart of the growing frustration. For millions of students, the question is no longer just whether examinations are conducted fairly.It is whether years of education, expensive coaching, repeated attempts at competitive exams and immense financial sacrifices will eventually lead to a secure, well-paying job. Without that, the frustrations exposed by such protests are likely to persist long after the headlines fade.
Article Summary: The number of young graduates in india has increased nearly 13-fold, rising from around 5 million in 1983 to 63 million in 2023. But while the supply of graduates has grown rapidly, employment opportunities have not kept pace. Graduate unemployment among people below the age of 25 is now close to 40%.

Article Title: Sun Pharma withdraws 11 eye medicines
Article Text:
The products covered are Depopred 2ml, Brinolar (BKC Free), Brinzotim Eye Drops 5ml (BKC Free), Lotepred 5ml, Lotepred 1% Eye Drops 5ml, Lotepred LS 0.2% Eye Drops 5ml, Lotepred T, Nepalact OD Eye Drops 3ml, Nepalact-Z, Toba-F and Nepalact E/D 5ml

NEW DELHI: Eleven ophthalmic products marketed by Sun Pharma have been withdrawn after the company's distribution arm directed retailers to stop further supply and withdraw existing stocks from the trade channel, according to a communication accessed by TOI. The July 17 communication instructed distributors to discontinue further distribution of the products.The products covered are Depopred 2ml, Brinolar (BKC Free), Brinzotim Eye Drops 5ml (BKC Free), Lotepred 5ml, Lotepred 1% Eye Drops 5ml, Lotepred LS 0.2% Eye Drops 5ml, Lotepred T, Nepalact OD Eye Drops 3ml, Nepalact-Z, Toba-F and Nepalact E/D 5ml. These medicines are widely prescribed for glaucoma, post-operative inflammation, allergic eye diseases and bacterial eye infections.Responding to TOI, a Sun Pharma spokesperson said: "We have initiated a proactive voluntary withdrawal of some ophthalmic products as a matter of abundant precaution. Product quality and patient safety are important to us." The company, however, did not specify the reason for the withdrawal of products or clarify whether it was linked to any manufacturing or quality issue.
Article Summary: Eleven ophthalmic products marketed by sun pharma have been withdrawn. Distribution arm directed retailers to stop further supply and withdraw existing stocks. These medicines are widely prescribed for glaucoma, post-operative inflammation, allergic eye diseases and bacterial eye infections.

Article Title: CBI files EPFO cheating case against Anil Ambani
Article Text:

MUMBAI: CBI lodged a cheating case against Reliance Capital Ltd (RCL), its ex-chairman Anil Ambani and unknown public servants in the alleged Rs 1,816 crore loss caused to Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO).CBI alleged that EPFO invested Rs 2,500 crore in RCL’s secured non-convertible debentures in 2013-14 and the company subsequently defaulted on repayment.Earlier, the issue was settled before National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), but recently ED shared its investigation finding of RCL’s fraudulent transactions. Based on this, EPFO subsequently filed a fraud case with CBI against Ambani and RCL.A spokesperson of Anil Ambani said, “The FIR registered by CBI pertains to Reliance Capital Limited. Ambani served as a non-executive director/chairman of the Board of Reliance Capital Limited from 2005 until Nov 2021, when Reserve Bank of India superseded the board of directors of the company and appointed an administrator. Ambani denies any wrongdoing, whatsoever, and reserves all rights available to him in law. ”EPFO administered the Employees’ Provident Fund, Pension Scheme and Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme.The fund accumulations with EPFO were vested in Central Board of Trustees (CBT), the statutory governing body which held, managed and invested such funds in trust for benefit of the subscribers.RCL’s financial position deteriorated in 2019, and the company subsequently went into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process.In 2021, EPFO lodged its claim before the resolution professional and, after NCLT approval in 2024, EPFO received Rs 1,492 crore of its total dues. The remaining amount of Rs 1,007 crore, along with Rs 809 crore interest, remained unpaid.ED, which probed RCL in a separate case, recently shared its findings with EPFO.EPFO said in its complaint to CBI that “the conduct of and transactions entered into Reliance Capital Limited and the persons in charge of its management during the period 7 Dec 2019 to 6 Dec 2021 disclose various fraudulent transactions...”
Article Summary: Cbi alleged that epfo invested rs 2,500 crore in rcl’s secured non-convertible debentures in 2013-14 and the company subsequently defaulted on repayment. Anil ambani served as a non-executive director/chairman of the board of reliance capital limited from 2005 until nov 2021.

Article Title: E20: AAP plans pro-choice rally to PM residence
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Stepping up his campaign against the rollout of E20 fuel, AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal Saturday announced a march to PM’s residence Tuesday to submit petitions against the ethanol-blended fuel programme, while demanding that consumers be given the option to choose betw-een pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations.Addressing AAP’s ‘National Townhall Against E20’ at Constitution Club, Kejriwal alleged Centre had “imposed” ethanol-blended fuel on consumers without adequate consultation and claimed it was causing financial losses to vehicle owners. He said petitions would be collected Monday, before a delegation of about 100 people marches to PM’s residence the following day.Kejriwal placed three demands before Centre -- provide both pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations, price E20 lower than pure petrol, and reduce petrol prices to below Rs 84 per litre. He argued that consumers should be free to decide which fuel they wish to purchase.Claiming govt has repeatedly maintained E20 is safe for vehicles, Kejriwal challenged Centre to make public the scientific studies supporting the policy. “Govt keeps saying studies have found E20 does not damage vehicles. If such studies exist, they should place the reports in the public domain,” he said, adding that several people had shared experiences of reduced mileage and vehicle problems during the town hall.He also alleged govt was only delaying the introduction of higher ethanol blends like E25 and E30 until the controversy surrounding E20 subsides. “There are no studies going on. They are simply waiting for the issue to die down. Once it settles, they will bring E25, E30 and continue increasing the ethanol content,” Kejriwal claimed, advising consumers to opt for electric vehicles until E100-compatible vehicles become commercially available.At the town hall, several owners, mechanics, delivery workers and experts claimed E20 had affected vehicle performance, increased maintenance costs and reduced mileage. Among them was a couple who commute daily from Delhi to Gurgaon. The husband said their 2014 petrol car earlier delivered 14 km per litre but now gives about 9 km per litre, significantly increasing monthly fuel expenses. His wife, who works in the automobile sector, claimed dealerships were receiving complaints from owners of newly-purchased vehicles regarding mileage and performance, but employees had no clear answers to offer.Motorcycle mechanic Aamir Khan, who has been repairing petrol vehicles for over a decade at Bhalswa Dairy, claimed he had witnessed a rise in complaints, particularly from owners of older BS-III and BS-IV vehicles. He advised owners to keep their fuel tanks relatively full to minimise air and moisture accumulation inside the tank.Dr Anupam Saini, an environmental scientist from DU, questioned the environmental benefits of ethanol, saying any assessment should account for fertiliser use, water consumption, land-use change and the overall carbon footprint of ethanol production rather than tailpipe emissions alone.
Article Summary: Aap national convener arvind kejriwal saturday announced a march to pm’s residence tuesday to submit petitions against the ethanol-blended fuel programme. He demanded that consumers be given the option to choose betw-een pure petrol and e20 at fuel stations.

Article Title: July GST collections up 15.4% to Rs 2.1 L cr on higher imports
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: GST collections rose 15.4% to Rs 2,11,205 crore in July, the second highest since the new structure was implemented last Sept, on the back of a 29% jump in integrated GST (IGST) on imports. This was also the highest pace of growth since rate rationalisation.The rise in IGST on imports in July (for transactions in the previous month) may be attributed to higher prices of crude and other commodities in the wake of the West Asia conflict.The impact of strong economic activity in June, when factory output grew at its fastest pace in nearly two years, was also visible on the tax numbers, seen as an advance indicator of economic activity. Some of the price hikes in FMCG and automobile sectors would have also buoyed collections. Central GST mop-up was pegged 12.3% higher at just under Rs 40,000 crore, while state GST grew 8.7% to nearly Rs 48,000 crore."The high GST collections tie in very well with the 7.3% increase in industrial production during June. It reflects continued economic resilience despite the challenges in the external environment...Thesteady growth in GST collections each month indicates that overall domestic consumption is becoming largely insulated from seasonal variations and external headwinds," said MS Mani, partner at Deloitte India.Some experts, however, are worried about the continued rise in imports. "...one cannot ignore the elevated levels of import GST collections, which remain a nagging concern. This points to a persistent gap in domestic manufacturing capability despite the range of successful PLI and Atmanirbhar Bharat interventions rolled out over the past few years.It is likely that the sustained push by policymakers towards localisation of around 100 products (being talked about) over a period of time will help bridge this gap," said Saurabh Agarwal, partner at EY India, a consulting firm.Net of refunds, which were 13% higher at almost Rs 30,000 crore, collections went up 15.8% to Rs 1,81,237 crore.Haryana logged the highest growth of 28%, followed by Gujarat and Puducherry (26%), Karnataka and Goa (23%), and Maharashtra (20%). Chhattisgarh (23% fall), Jharkhand and Manipur (20% decline) were among the laggards.
Article Summary: Gst collections rose 15.4% to rs 2,11,205 crore in july, the second highest since the new structure was implemented last sept. The rise in igst on imports in july (for transactions in the previous month) may be attributed to higher prices of crude and other commodities in the wake of the west asia conflict.

Article Title: DSC A24 : Indian Navy launches 5th diving support craft ‘DSC A24’, ship to boost underwater diving ops
Article Text: NEW DELHI: In a boost for the Indian Navy 's underwater diving operations, the fifth vessel of the diving support craft project, DSC A24, was successfully launched in Kolkata on Saturday. The launch of DSC A24 comes just days after the delivery of the diving support vessel (DSV) Nipun to the Navy.A DSC is a specialised small-to-medium naval or commercial vessel built to facilitate underwater diving operations, inspections, repairs and salvage work in coastal and harbour environments. While a DSC is used for shallow and coastal-water diving tasks, a DSV is a massive, ocean-going capital ship equipped for deep-sea saturation diving and submarine rescue operations.In an X post, an Indian Navy spokesperson said, "Fifth ship of DSC Project, DSC A24, was launched on 01 Aug 26 at M/s Titagarh Rail Systems Limited, Kolkata, by Mrs Kamal Singh in presence of Vice Admiral Gurcharan Singh, Chief of Personnel."The DSCs are being constructed by TRSL under the IRS and Naval rules, with a catamaran-hull form and displacement in the range of 300-400 tonnes, Navy said."DSC A24 is equipped with state-of-the-art diving systems and is tailor-made for conducting operational dives. A testament to engineering excellence and indigenous capability, these ships are proud flag bearers of Make in India initiative, strengthening Indian Navy's off-shore diving capabilities," Navy said on X.
Article Summary: The launch of dsc a24 comes just days after the delivery of the diving support vessel (dsv) nipun to the navy. A dsc is a specialised small-to-medium naval or commercial vessel built to facilitate underwater diving operations.

Article Title: Petrol would've hit Rs 125/litre in Delhi without ethanol blend, says govt
Article Text:
The petroleum ministry defended ethanol blending, stating it saved consumers nearly thirty rupees per litre.





NEW DELHI: Petrol in Delhi would have cost around Rs 125 a litre when global crude prices touched $135 a barrel, had oil companies not blended ethanol into the fuel, the petroleum ministry said on Friday, defending the ethanol programme against claims about its costs, food security impact, and alleged taxpayer subsidy.The ministry said consumers instead paid Rs 94.77 per litre, since ethanol — procured domestically at pre-agreed prices — made up 20% of every litre and helped insulate retail prices from the crude spike, saving nearly Rs 30 a litre at the peak of the crisis.The government held petrol and diesel prices steady for nearly 75 days after the West Asia conflict began on February 28, before raising them by Rs 7.5 a litre in May. Standard E20 petrol (91-octane) now costs Rs 102.12 a litre in Delhi, while 100-octane petrol is priced at Rs 169.The ministry also denied allegations that foodgrain meant for the poor was being diverted for ethanol production, or that subsidised FCI rice was being used to support the programme.On the question of fuel efficiency, the road transport ministry — citing a study by ARAI, SIAM and IOC — told the Lok Sabha on Thursday that BS-III, BS-IV and BS-VI vehicles designed for E10 fuel may see efficiency drop by 2-6% depending on vehicle category and age when run on E20.The oil ministry had earlier told the Rajya Sabha on July 20 that the reduction in such vehicles is limited to about 3-5%.Both ministries said the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme was rolled out through a phased, scientifically validated process, with blending levels raised gradually as production capacity and infrastructure were built up. Road transport minister Nitin Gadkari told the Lok Sabha that the shift to E20 followed validation of fuel systems, engine durability, drivability, material compatibility and emissions performance, with automakers, oil marketing companies, and the sugar and grain industries consulted throughout.The government added that lab studies and real-world data have shown no adverse impact on vehicle performance from E20 fuel, noting that over 20 crore two-wheelers and 3 crore-plus petrol cars have run on these blends without verified evidence of engine failure linked to ethanol blending.
Article Summary: Petrol in delhi would have cost around rs 125 a litre when global crude prices touched $135 a barrel, had oil companies not blended ethanol into the fuel. The government held petrol and diesel prices steady for nearly 75 days after the west asia conflict began on february 28.

Article Title: Sridhar Vembu raises AI ‘wiping’ jobs question; says: We need to find answers
Article Text:
Sridhar Vembu

Vembu feels Sam Altman’s Universal Basic Income can be a solution



Read Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu’s complete post here



The real issue facing our nation is how to create jobs for our massive cohort of youth in this very uncertain global landscape.

Sadly, the IT industry, including Zoho, have not created many jobs in recent years. We have not laid off people but we are not creating new jobs either.

The money that would have gone to new employees is now going to AI and data center costs, the latter due to the steep rise in server and memory prices. We are trying to control those costs but a lot of that is out of our control.

While AI allows us to produce more software quicker, does the over-saturated global software market need a lot more software? Like any commodity industry, the focus shifts to quality, reliability, brand and so on and growth will be much slower.

Software customers (large and mid-sized enterprises) also have redireced their own IT spending towards AI. Even the AI companies which are growing very rapidly are borrowing and spending huge amounts of money in capex, and it is not clear they will achieve the massive profits they need to justify all the capex.

What other industry can pick up the slack? Extensive automation means that large scale manufacturing produces few jobs.

As an economic thinker, this is a good thing: ultimately all kinds of goods, including advanced tech products become very affordable because production becomes so cheap. The "only" question is how the economy is structured so people have the income to afford those affordable goods.

That "only" question, simple in theory, is not easy in practice. Some people think the answer is Universal Basic Income (UBI) and some of that is already happening in India (we call them freebies). We can expect the political pressure to do a lot more.

Is there a better answer? Continued ...

Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu has publicly raised concerns about artificial intelligence ‘wiping’ jobs, warning that India must urgently find answers to safeguard its massive youth workforce. In a post shared on social media platform X(formerly known as Twitter) Vembu mentioned that the real issue facing the nation right now is how to create jobs in an uncertain global landscape, noting that the IT industry including Zoho has not generated any significant new employment in the recent years. Vembu further explained that money which was once earmarked for new employees is now being spent on AI and rising data center costs, driven by steep increases in server and memory prices. He further noted that while Zoho has avoided layoffs, but admitted that the company is also not expanding its workforce. “AI allows us to produce more software quicker, but does the over-saturated global software market need a lot more software?” he asked, adding that growth in the sector will be slower as focus shifts to quality and brand.Vembu further argued that while automation makes goods cheaper and more accessible, the challenge is ensuing people have income to afford them.He also pointed to Universal Basic Income (UBI) as one possible solution, referencing Sam Altman’s $14 million investment into UBI research. “Some people think the answer is UBI, and some of that is already happening in India — we call them freebies. We can expect the political pressure to do a lot more. Is there a better answer?” Vembu asked.For those unaware, Sam Altman’s Universal Basic Income (UBI) theory is rooted in the idea that as artificial intelligence and automation eliminate traditional jobs, societies will need a safety net to ensure people can still afford basic necessities. He believes UBI — guaranteed cash payments to all citizens — could be one of the most viable solutions. As CEO of OpenAI, Altman has long warned that AI could displace millions of jobs. He argues that while automation makes goods cheaper, people still need income to buy them. Altman invested $14 million through OpenResearch, alongside $10 million from OpenAI, to run one of the largest UBI trials in the U.S.
Article Summary: Zoho co-founder sridhar vembu has publicly raised concerns about artificial intelligence ‘wiping’ jobs, warning that india must urgently find answers to safeguard its massive youth workforce. He also pointed to universal basic income as one possible solution, referencing sam altman’s $14 million investment into ubi research.

Article Title: Christian Kleinerman, EVP of Product, Snowflake: Future belongs to organizations who can give AI the trusted enterprise context
Article Text:
Q. Snowflake has positioned itself as the platform where enterprise data and AI come together. As every major cloud and AI company is trying to become the orchestration layer for enterprise AI, what differentiates Snowflake's vision of the "agentic control plane", and why should enterprises trust you with that role?

Q. Many companies are experimenting with AI agents, but governance, security and compliance remain major hurdles. Do you believe most enterprises are actually ready for autonomous agents today? What capabilities has Snowflake built to ensure AI agents remain auditable, secure and within policy boundaries?

Q. Enterprise CIOs are under pressure to justify AI investments with measurable business outcomes. Can you share specific examples—globally and from India—where Snowflake customers have demonstrated tangible ROI from AI deployments, and what metrics matter most?

Q. The AI landscape is becoming increasingly fragmented, with enterprises choosing between proprietary and open-source models while traditional SaaS is also being reshaped. How does Snowflake plan to stay relevant in a world where foundation models are rapidly commoditising, and what advice do you give customers on selecting the right models for different workloads?

Q. India has emerged as one of the world's fastest-growing AI and digital infrastructure markets. Where does India fit in Snowflake's long-term global strategy—in terms of customers, engineering talent, partnerships and product innovation—and what new investments or priorities should we expect over the next few years?

AI Data Cloud company Snowflake aims to make it easy for enterprises to innovate faster and get more value from data. Times of India spoke to Christian Kleinerman who serves as Snowflake’s EVP of Product and has been with the company since 2018. He oversees the company’s global product strategy and vision. Christian is a database expert with over 20 years of experience working with various database technologies and has more than 15 years of management and leadership experience. Most recently, Christian worked at Google leading YouTube’s infrastructure and data systems. Prior to that, he served as General Manager of the Data Warehousing product unit at Microsoft where he was responsible for a broad portfolio of products. Christian holds a BS in Industrial Engineering from Los Andes University in Colombia, and he is a named inventor on numerous Snowflake patents. Kleinerman's spoke about AI agents, Snowflake's role in the AI era, company's India market and more.The industry is gradually realizing that powerful models alone aren't enough.Models are improving at a remarkable pace, and increasingly interchangeable. The real challenge for enterprises is giving those models the context they need to make useful decisions. If you think about how work actually gets done inside a company, context comes from more than just data. It comes from business definitions, governance policies, security, operational systems, permissions, and the relationships between them.That's where Snowflake fits. We've spent more than a decade helping enterprises solve problems like governance, access control, lineage, compliance, and interoperability. Our strategy isn't to build the best foundation model or create another closed ecosystem. At Snowflake we are committed to give our customers access to the leading frontier and open source models even as the leaderboards evolve. This allows enterprises to maintain flexibility and maximize value of their AI initiatives.We have delivered capabilities to ensure that agents can be identified in Snowflake, so their activity and accessible permissions can be customized to the level of privilege desired for an agent. And not every company is ready for autonomous agents, but we see some companies at the forefront creating real business value. Agents summarize information, answer business questions, turn insights into action, and help people complete work much faster.Before an agent updates a CRM record, approves a payment, or triggers a business workflow, organisations need confidence that every action happens within the same governance capabilities and guarantees that applies to people modifying those same systems. They need auditability, clear permissions, and policy enforcement. That's an area where Snowflake starts from a position of strength. Governance has always been built into the platform. Every AI interaction inherits the same role-based access controls, lineage, audit trails, and security policies that already protect enterprise data.We believe autonomy will happen incrementally based on customers’ comfort with AI. Some will begin with agents that recommend actions, introduce human approval where appropriate, and gradually automate more as confidence grows. The future belongs to organizations who can give AI the trusted enterprise context and guardrails needed to operate safely at scale.Enterprise AI success is ultimately measured by business outcomes, not AI adoption or model benchmarks. CIOs should focus on tangible metrics such as faster deployment, lower costs, improved productivity, and better customer experiences.We're already seeing customers achieve that in production. Providence Health is using Snowflake Cortex AI to extract insights from clinical notes more quickly, helping clinicians make faster decisions. Thomson Reuters is applying AI to legal and compliance workflows, accelerating how professionals work with complex regulatory information. And organisations like DTCC, Wakefit and Urban Company are using our solutions.We also believe it's important to use these technologies ourselves. More than 6,000 Snowflake employees now use our GTM AI Assistant every week, handling over 30,000 questions across sales and marketing. Tasks like researching customers, writing SQL, and preparing for meetings used to require significant manual effort, and now they happen in minutes. Those are the kinds of productivity gains we want our customers to achieve as well. By powering internal operations and decision-making through Snowflake CoWork and CoCo, we rigorously test, refine, and prove our products before bringing them to customers, supporting over 8,000 employees worldwide in product delivery, development, and sales productivity.We're moving into a world where traditional software is being disrupted and AI is becoming the primary interface that people use to interact with data and applications. As that happens, foundation models will continue to improve rapidly, costs will come down, and customers will have more choice than ever before.Snowflake has built its strategy around that reality. Rather than asking customers to commit to a single model or AI provider, Snowflake is deliberately model-agnostic. We work across the leading proprietary and open-source models because we don’t want our customers to be locked into any one vendor. We want them to take advantage of whichever models are best as the technology evolves.In this new era, what doesn't commoditise is enterprise data and enterprise context. In order to perform reliably in an enterprise, models will always need trusted data, business semantics, governance, security, and operational context fueling them. That's where we see Snowflake's role. We provide the trusted data foundation that allows customers to adopt new models without having to rethink their entire AI strategy every time the technology changes.My advice to customers is to optimize for business outcomes, not model preferences. Use the right model for the right workload. Smaller, more efficient models are often ideal for tasks like classification or information extraction, while frontier models are best suited for more complex reasoning and planning. The important thing is building an architecture that gives you the flexibility to evolve as the model landscape evolves. That's exactly why we've taken an open, model-agnostic approach from the beginning.India is one of our most important strategic markets because it brings together four things that are critical for the AI era: a vibrant digital economy, robust public digital infrastructure, world-class engineering talent, and enterprises that are modernising rapidly, along with a growing number of our global customers who are setting up their Global Capability Centre (GCC) base. Over the past year, Snowflake has doubled its sales team in India and 50% of its APJ partners are based here, underscoring the country’s pivotal position in our global strategy and its vast, expanding data and AI market.
Article Summary: Ai data cloud company snowflake aims to make it easy for enterprises to innovate faster and get more value from data. Christian kleinerman is snowflake’s evp of product and has been with the company since 2018. He oversees the company's global product strategy and vision.

Article Title: Apple's India story is no longer just about iPhones, the next phase has started
Article Text:
Disclaimer: It's an AI-generated image

Factors that made the difference

Real upside lies elsewhere and is showing

There are, of course, reasons for caution

For years, Apple's quarterly earnings followed a familiar script in India. Tim Cook would mention "strong growth", analysts would point to iPhone sales, and the conversation would end there. This quarter felt different. Yes, Apple reported another record June quarter in India. Yes, the iPhone remained the company's biggest revenue generator globally, contributing nearly half of total revenue. But hidden inside the earnings call was a more important signal: India is gradually becoming a multi-product Apple market.That may sound obvious. It isn't. Apple CFO Kevan Parekh devoted unusual attention to the Mac business, saying Mac revenue hit a record $10.4 billion globally, up 29%, driven by the MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro. India wasn't merely name-checked. It was among the markets that saw the best quarter ever for new Mac customers and people upgrading existing Macs.That matters because one can argue that Macs have always been Apple's toughest sell in India. Unlike smartphones, laptops have longer replacement cycles, fewer financing options and far lower aspirational value. Convincing someone to spend over Rs 1 lakh on a laptop is significantly harder than persuading them to buy a premium phone on a two-year EMI.If Macs are now finding scale in India, Apple is winning a different kind of customer. The reasons aren't difficult to spot.The biggest catalyst has been the MacBook Neo. Apple has spent years trying to make Macs feel more accessible without making them feel cheaper. Neo appears to have struck that balance. Students, first-time professionals and families looking for a long-lasting computer suddenly have an Apple option that doesn't immediately feel financially intimidating.The second factor is Apple's pricing strategy. While most smartphone brands have quietly increased prices over the past year because of rising component costs and a weaker rupee, Apple largely chose not to. It absorbed the cost pressures instead. That's a luxury only a company sitting on one of the largest cash piles in corporate history can afford. The result is subtle but powerful.When competitors become more expensive, Apple doesn't necessarily have to become cheaper. It simply has to stay where it is. Couple that with aggressive exchange offers, no-cost EMIs, student discounts and bank cashback programmes, and Apple's premium products begin looking surprisingly attainable. The interesting part is that Apple is no longer selling isolated devices. It is selling an ecosystem.An iPhone owner becomes more likely to consider a Mac. A Mac user is nudged towards AirPods. Then perhaps an iPad. Eventually come AppleCare, iCloud storage and services subscriptions. Every new hardware customer is effectively the first step in a much larger revenue journey. That is exactly why the Mac numbers deserve more attention than the iPhone numbers. The iPhone business in India is already relatively mature by Apple's standards. Growth will continue, but largely through premiumisation and higher market share within the premium segment.India still has enormous headroom in personal computers, tablets, wearables and services. Even modest gains across these categories can create a much larger business than simply selling more iPhones. Apple's expanding retail footprint reinforces that strategy. Six company-owned stores across major cities, with more planned, aren't just sales outlets. They're experience centres. They introduce customers to products they may never have actively considered buying online.This also reflects Apple's growing confidence in India as more than a manufacturing destination. Much has been written about iPhone assembly shifting to India. That story is important, but investors sometimes confuse manufacturing with consumption. The two don't necessarily move together.This quarter suggests both are beginning to strengthen simultaneously. India is emerging as one of Apple's most important production hubs while also becoming one of its fastest-growing consumer markets. Few countries offer both opportunities at the same time.Apple still remains overwhelmingly dependent on premium consumers. Its market share by volume is tiny compared to Android brands. The company's success depends on affluent urban buyers continuing to spend despite economic uncertainty. Competition is also becoming sharper. Samsung remains formidable in premium smartphones. AI-powered Windows laptops are improving rapidly. Chinese brands continue to innovate aggressively on hardware.And Apple's next big test may arrive with foldables. Reports suggest the company's first foldable iPhone will initially be manufactured in China rather than India. That may not matter immediately for Indian consumers, but it highlights that Apple is still selective about where it places its most advanced manufacturing.None of that changes the larger takeaway from this quarter. The most important number wasn't revenue, profit or even iPhone sales. It was the fact that Apple talked about India not as a fast-growing smartphone market, but as a market where customers are increasingly buying into the entire Apple experience.That's a far more durable business than selling another iPhone. And for India, it suggests the company's next phase of growth may be defined less by one iconic product and more by an ecosystem quietly taking root.
Article Summary: Apple reported another record june quarter in india. Mac revenue hit a record $10.4 billion globally, up 29%. The biggest catalyst has been the macbook neo. Apple is no longer selling isolated devices. It is selling an ecosystem. An iphone owner becomes more likely to consider a mac. A mac user is nudged towards airpods.

Article Title: Chinese military-linked researchers are trying to transfer that expensive, proprietary reasoning from Western models into smaller systems they can control and deploy locally
Article Text:
Chinese military-linked researchers are trying to transfer that expensive, proprietary reasoning from Western models into smaller systems they can control and deploy locally

Chinese military researchers use US AI models for distillation

OpenAI and Anthropic models reportedly used in Chinese research

Distilled AI models tested for drones and military operations, claims report

Distillation does not fully reproduce frontier AI capabilities

Chinese military-linked researchers have used outputs from advanced American AI models made by OpenAI and Anthropic to train their own systems, according to a Reuters review of more than 80 Chinese academic papers and patents. The findings come after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei raised concerns about China potentially using distillation to draw capabilities from powerful US frontier AI models. Reuters found that researchers linked to China’s military and security institutions have used a technique called “model distillation” to transfer selected capabilities and reasoning from US models into smaller systems that can be controlled and deployed locally, including for defence-related applications.According to Reuters, the documents provide a look at how institutions linked to China’s military are using advanced US AI models while Washington tries to restrict Beijing’s access to advanced chips and other technologies. The research included material compiled by the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, and found widespread use of model distillation among researchers linked to the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and other military institutions.For those unaware, model distillation is a widely used AI technique in which the output of a powerful AI model is used to train a smaller model. This can allow the smaller system to gain selected capabilities without requiring the massive computing resources needed to build a frontier AI model from scratch.A paper published last year by researchers from PLA Unit 96941, described by Reuters as a military intelligence and cyber-warfare unit in Beijing, detailed the use of OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 to process sensitive military source code.The researchers said third-party AI models were not suitable for directly handling classified information. They instead used GPT-3.5 to summarise software code and trained a domestic AI model using those summaries. The resulting system could then operate inside Chinese military networks, according to the report.Researchers at the North University of China also used Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku to create synthetic training data for a model designed for social media monitoring and content moderation, Reuters reported.Anthropic told Reuters that it does not offer commercial access to Claude in China or to companies controlled by Beijing. The company also warned that distilled models may not retain the safety safeguards built into the original system, potentially allowing some capabilities to move into models outside its control.According to the documents, the use of model distillation extended to other defence applications. A 2024 paper from the PLA’s National University of Defense Technology described using distillation to reduce the size of an image-processing AI model so that it could run aboard unmanned aerial vehicles. The approach allowed drones to analyse live video and assist with navigation and targeting even when communications were unavailable.Researchers at China’s Academy of Military Sciences similarly used distillation to operate a target-recognition model on tactical hardware during simulated maritime operations involving drones, ships and unmanned submarines, according to a study published earlier this year.China has promoted technologies including “model lightweighting” and edge computing as it faces US restrictions on access to advanced chips. Such technologies can help AI models operate on devices including drones and satellites with limited computing power.However, the dispute between the US and China is focused on the alleged unauthorised extraction of capabilities rather than model distillation itself. Sunny Cheung, a Jamestown fellow who analysed more than 60 papers, told Reuters that Chinese military researchers were attempting to capture the reasoning abilities of Western AI models.“Teaching a model the right answer is one thing but teaching it the reasoning behind the answer is much harder,” Cheung said. “These papers show Chinese military-linked researchers are trying to transfer that expensive, proprietary reasoning from Western models into smaller systems they can control and deploy locally,” he added.Despite its potential benefits, experts said model distillation has limits. Smaller models generally inherit selected capabilities from their larger “teacher” models rather than reproducing their full intelligence.Trevor Koverko, co-founder of AI data company Sapien, told Reuters: “It is best understood as transferring selected capabilities into a cheaper, locally controlled system, not achieving independence from frontier AI.”Chinese military researchers are also studying the security risks created by distillation. Researchers at the Army Engineering University published a paper in January examining “data-free distillation,” which can be used to reverse-engineer some capabilities of an AI model without accessing its underlying parameters.
Article Summary: Chinese military-linked researchers have used advanced us ai models to train their own systems, according to a reuters review of more than 80 chinese academic papers and patents. Researchers linked to china’s military and security institutions have used a technique called ‘model distillation’ to transfer capabilities and reasoning from us models into smaller systems that can be controlled and deployed locally.
